changes.new: ## Tool-call matching and task completion A correct API name, a correct argument and a completed task provide different feedback. Suppose the requested action is to check a fare from ORD to SFO. The call `Get_Price(loc_1="ORD", loc_2="LAX")` uses the right function and the right departure airport, but asks about the wrong destination. An exact-match reward treats it like a completely unrelated call. A decomposed reward can credit the fields that match while still withholding full credit. ### ToolRL: compare the function and its arguments ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/toolrl/reward-design.png]] *Cheng Qian et al., ToolRL. [Original repository illustration](https://github.com/qiancheng0/ToolRL/blob/8cee13ec0ca72f0461da372a93a6fd8140dbb840/assets/reward.png), Apache 2.0; the full 6696 × 2365 image is retained without changes. The upper part separates format from correctness. The lower part compares function names, parameter names and values for two candidate outputs. The [license is included with the site](/licenses/toolrl-8cee13ec-Apache-2.0.txt). Open the original to read the individual fields.* The released [reward implementation](https://github.com/qiancheng0/ToolRL/blob/8cee13ec0ca72f0461da372a93a6fd8140dbb840/verl/utils/reward_score/rlla.py) first compares the lists of function names. Its `match_score` counts repeated names: two calls to `Get_Price` and one call to `Get_Price` have intersection size 1 and union size 2, not two identical sets of names. For matching calls, the implementation adds the Jaccard score of their parameter names and the number of equal values under the same keys. The raw score is then rescaled to the configured interval. In the default correctness range, a raw score `S` becomes $$ \begin{aligned} S_{\max}&=1+|G|+\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{keys}(g)|,\\ R_{\mathrm{correct}}&=6\,\frac{S}{S_{\max}}-3. \end{aligned} $$ Here `G` is the list of ground-truth calls, not a GRPO group size. For one expected call with two parameters, the maximum is `1 + 1 + 2 = 4`. The incorrect-destination call earns 1 for its function name, 1 for its parameter-name set and 1 for the departure value: `S=3` and `R_correct=1.5`. An exact call earns 3. A completely different function earns −3, even if its arguments happen to contain the same strings. The following code handles only one expected call and one predicted call, with ordinary JSON scalar values. It exposes the arithmetic without implementing the multi-call assignment problem. ```python def single_tool_reward(gold, predicted): gold_args, predicted_args = gold["parameters"], predicted["parameters"] if gold["name"] != predicted["name"]: return -3.0 gkeys, pkeys = set(gold_args), set(predicted_args) union = gkeys | pkeys key_score = len(gkeys & pkeys) / len(union) if union else 1.0 value_score = sum( k in predicted_args and predicted_args[k] == v for k, v in gold_args.items() ) raw = 1.0 + key_score + value_score maximum = 2 + len(gold_args) return 6 * raw / maximum - 3 fare_gold = { "name": "Get_Price", "parameters": {"loc_1": "ORD", "loc_2": "SFO"}, } fare_wrong_destination = { "name": "Get_Price", "parameters": {"loc_1": "ORD", "loc_2": "LAX"}, } assert single_tool_reward(fare_gold, fare_gold) == 3.0 assert single_tool_reward(fare_gold, fare_wrong_destination) == 1.5 assert single_tool_reward(fare_gold, {"name": "Delete", "parameters": {}}) == -3.0 print("correctness:", single_tool_reward(fare_gold, fare_wrong_destination)) ``` Format contributes a separate 0 or 1 in the default code; the optional length reward is off unless enabled. A correctly formatted wrong-destination call therefore receives `1 + 1.5 = 2.5`, versus 4 for a correctly formatted exact call. This is partial feedback, not a certificate that the requested task succeeded. Tracking the success rate separately prevents a rising average reward from concealing errors in destinations or other critical arguments. For several calls, matching itself needs verification. [ToolRL §3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.13958v1#S3.SS3) describes an optimal assignment, whereas the pinned code greedily consumes one unused prediction per ground-truth call. With repeated function names, the first local choice can prevent a better overall assignment. Reordering candidates can then change the implemented reward. An experiment must identify which procedure it ran; the paper's formula and a repository function are not interchangeable. Matching against one annotated call sequence also penalizes valid alternatives unless the evaluator explicitly allows them. A different route through an API can reach the same final state. Conversely, matching every annotated field cannot establish compliance with a requirement that the annotation omitted. For state-changing tasks, final-state checks and action-policy checks remain necessary. Binary matching is another choice. In [Tool-N1 §4.1–4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.00024v2#S4.SS3), an answer earns 1 only when the required tags and the function's name and argument-value dictionary are correct. Reordering dictionary keys is allowed. Our wrong-destination example therefore earns 0, not partial credit. Multi-turn source trajectories are split into single-step prediction records with the preceding interaction supplied as context; this is not full online optimization of a newly executed trajectory. The choice of initialization is empirical too. In [Tool-N1 §5.3.2, Table 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.00024v2#S5.SS3.SSS2), the 5,518-instance comparison reports averages of 83.17 for SFT followed by RL and 83.24 for RL alone under its data allocations. This small reported difference does not establish that SFT generally harms tool learning. Both recipes start from an already instruction-tuned model. ### Partial completion and unnecessary calls ASTRA uses verified subtask completion and a trajectory-level F1-style reward. For `n` required subtasks, `s` completed subtasks and `c` calls, $$ \begin{aligned} r&=s/n,\qquad p=s/(c+\epsilon),\\ F_1&=\frac{2pr}{p+r}. \end{aligned} $$ Its reported recall-only and precision-only ablations exhibit different over-calling and under-calling failures. These are results of that experiment, not guarantees that F1 stabilizes every agent. The authors also omit KL and entropy bonuses, filter groups with degenerate reward variance, and buffer surplus usable samples for subsequent batches. See [ASTRA §3.1, §3.2.2 and §4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21558v1#S3.SS1). Consider a constructed task with four independent checks, each obtainable by one call. Completing two checks with two calls has recall 0.5, precision 1 and F1 ≈ 0.667. Completing all four with four calls earns 1. Completing the same four with eight calls leaves recall at 1 but lowers precision to 0.5 and F1 to about 0.667. For `s>0`, substitution reduces the expression to `2s / (n + c + epsilon)`. When `s=0`, define the reward as zero rather than evaluate `0/0`. The code below enforces the example's one-subtask-per-call assumption. It is not a general implementation of the ASTRA environment. ```python def completion_efficiency_reward(required, solved, calls, eps=1e-8): if any(type(x) is not int for x in (required, solved, calls)): raise ValueError("counts must be integers") if not (required > 0 and 0 <= solved <= required and calls >= solved): raise ValueError("require positive task size and solved <= calls") if not 0 < eps < float("inf"): raise ValueError("eps must be finite and positive") return 2 * solved / (required + calls + eps) if solved else 0.0 efficient_partial = completion_efficiency_reward(4, 2, 2) efficient_complete = completion_efficiency_reward(4, 4, 4) redundant_complete = completion_efficiency_reward(4, 4, 8) assert efficient_complete > efficient_partial assert efficient_complete > redundant_complete assert completion_efficiency_reward(4, 0, 0) == 0.0 print([round(x, 6) for x in (efficient_partial, efficient_complete, redundant_complete)]) ``` The denominator measures calls, not wall time, tokens, money or risk. Replacing one cheap call with one expensive call leaves this reward unchanged. A call that solves several subtasks would violate the example's assumption and could make the quantity called precision exceed 1. The subtask accounting and permitted tool semantics must therefore be specified before using the formula. ### Refusal, missing information and group filtering A task need not have one unique accepted answer. A verifier can accept several valid programs, routes or final states. It can also reward stopping without an action when an externally specified condition makes execution impermissible or impossible. For example, a synthetic calendar task can expose an explicit `authorized=false` flag to the environment. The evaluator checks that no write occurred and that the agent requested authorization. A successful unauthorized write receives zero; preserving the state and requesting permission receives one. This constructed rule is verifiable because authorization and state changes have specified representations. It does not establish that a program can decide arbitrary natural-language safety questions. If both actions instead receive zero, the reward supplies no distinction between them. A group-centred algorithm cannot recover that missing distinction. Filtering identical-reward groups removes their relative reward contribution regardless of whether the task was easy, impossible or poorly specified; it does not intrinsically prohibit learning refusals. The filtered fraction and the evaluation of unsolvable and unauthorized tasks must be reported separately. Finally, an executable training environment can model only some production failures. Evaluation should separately cover timeouts, rate limits, pagination, permissions, changing state and irreversible side effects. The availability of a training-time verifier also says nothing about which checks will be available when a deployed agent answers a new request. ## Проверка результата и проверка хода решения
